meta.ref: HEAD~1..HEAD (9ec23e4 — refunds: record as rows, rename order status to state)
meta.title: Refunds as rows, orders.status → state

intent: Refunds stop being an order status and become their own refunds table: docs/refunds.md argues that an order can be refunded more than once, so a single orders.status value cannot carry the fact. A new API endpoint records a refund row (and bumps a denormalized orders.refunded_cents), orders.status is renamed to state across the PHP API and the TypeScript worker, and the worker gains a settleRefunds step after shipping to pay recorded refunds out. What could break: the rename is done as DROP COLUMN status + ADD COLUMN state DEFAULT 'placed' with no backfill, so every existing order silently reverts to placed; the settle step is hooked in immediately after the state becomes shipped, which is exactly when the API first allows a refund, so nothing it could settle exists yet; and place() renames its response key, breaking every client at once.

groups.name: Schema: refunds table and the status→state swap
groups.why: The migration is the cause of every other file, and it renames a column by dropping it: existing orders lose their status with no backfill, and 0001 declared status TEXT NOT NULL with no default, so nothing can recover it afterwards. Read it first and decide whether that data loss is intended.

groups.name: The scope decisions this change is built on
groups.why: docs/refunds.md states the rules the code is supposed to obey — a refund is a row, order money never changes, refunds only after fulfilment, provider calls out of scope. Use it as the yardstick for everything else, and note the two places the code disagrees with it.

groups.name: Recording a refund (API)
groups.why: The controller's new refund action and the repository that inserts the row and bumps the denormalized counter. This is where the eligibility rule and the money arithmetic live — including the response field that reads a property the returned refund does not have.

groups.name: status → state call-sites
groups.why: Follow-through of the column rename across the PHP insert, the worker's guard and the db helper. Verify the pattern landed everywhere and that no reader of the old field survives — including the API response key that clients depend on.

groups.name: Settling refunds in the worker
groups.why: The worker's new settle step, its hook into fulfilment, and the tests that cover it. Check the idempotence claim and whether this code can execute at all: payout is called but never defined, and the stubs hide it.

groups.name: New refund configuration
groups.why: The repo's first .env.example introduces two refund knobs that would have to exist in every deployed environment — neither of which any code in this diff reads, so setting them changes nothing.

db/migrations/0002_refunds.sql.why: Creates refunds (order_id FK, cents with CHECK (cents > 0), reason, created_at) plus an index on order_id, adds the denormalized orders.refunded_cents, and renames status to state. Review focus: the rename is DROP COLUMN status followed by ADD COLUMN state ... DEFAULT 'placed' with no backfill — every existing order loses its real status and comes back as placed. In 0001 status was TEXT NOT NULL with no default, so there is nothing to recover it from afterwards. Review focus: the comment on refunded_cents says it is "kept in sync by the worker", but in this diff the only writer is the API (RefundRepository::record); the worker never touches it. Review focus: the table has no settled/paid column, so the worker's pendingRefunds/markSettled model has nothing in the schema to stand on, and there is no constraint bounding total refunds by orders.total_cents.

api/src/Controller/OrdersController.php.why: Takes RefundRepository as a second dependency, switches place()'s response key from status to state, and adds refund(): load the order, reject with 409 NOT_FULFILLED unless state === 'shipped', otherwise record the refund and return 201. Review focus: the response reports 'refunded_cents' => $refund->orderTotal — record() returns the freshly inserted refund row (order_id, cents, reason), which has no orderTotal, and the accumulated counter the caller expects is computed in SQL inside the transaction and never read back. Review focus: renaming the place() response key is a breaking change for every client, with no versioning or dual-key transition. Review focus: nothing validates $req->cents() before the insert, so a zero/negative amount or an amount above the recorded total surfaces as a database CHECK violation (a 500), not a 400.
frag: // Only fulfilled orders can be refunded — see docs/refunds.md.

api/src/Repository/RefundRepository.php.why: New repository: record() inserts the refund row and bumps orders.refunded_cents in one transaction, then returns the inserted refund. Review focus: this is the real owner of the denormalized counter — directly contradicting the migration comment that credits the worker; decide which component owns it before someone adds a second increment in the worker and double-counts. Review focus: the increment is unbounded — no read of total_cents, no row lock, no idempotency key, so repeated calls (client retry, duplicate request) each add another refund and push refunded_cents past the amount ever charged. The returned object carries no order-level total, which is what the controller then tries to read.

edges: The decision that an order can be refunded partially is what forces a separate refunds table instead of a value in the order's status.
Dropping orders.status forces the insert and the new find() onto the renamed column; the API breaks against the old schema and vice versa.
The worker reads the same column, so the rename has to land in its db helper and its fulfilment guard at the same time as the migration.
writes the row and the counter
The new table and the denormalized refunded_cents column are both written here — even though the migration's comment attributes the counter to the worker.
The API only records intent; the recorded rows are what settleRefunds is supposed to consume — but nothing in the worker reads the refunds table yet.
The hook runs right after the state is set to shipped, which is precisely before the API will accept any refund for that order — so it can never find one pending.
Both accessors were added as no-ops for this caller, and the refunds table has no settled marker for markSettled to set.

migrations: db/migrations/0002_refunds.sql — creates refunds + refunds_order_id_idx and adds orders.refunded_cents (safe, defaulted).

Same file, destructive: ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN status, then ADD COLUMN state NOT NULL DEFAULT 'placed'. Irreversible and unbackfilled — every existing order's real status is discarded and replaced by 'placed'. If existing orders matter, add the backfill (add state, UPDATE state FROM status, then drop) before this goes anywhere near production data.

Consequence for the new feature: after the migration no order is in state 'shipped', so the refund endpoint returns 409 NOT_FULFILLED for the entire pre-existing order history until fulfilment runs again.
deploy: No backward-compatible window exists: the API and the worker both read `state` only, and the old code reads `status` only. Migration and both services must go out together, or plan the rename as add-column + dual-write + backfill + drop.
Breaking API response: POST /orders now returns `state` instead of `status`. Coordinate with clients or ship both keys for one release.

The refund write path is live before the payout path works (undefined `payout`, stubbed pendingRefunds/markSettled). Expect refunds to accumulate as rows that are never paid — consider keeping the endpoint behind a flag until the worker actually settles.
ops.note: Nothing in this diff wires the two new REFUND_* variables to code, and there is no rollback for the status→state drop; the reversible part of the migration (refunds table, refunded_cents) is fine to roll forward, the column drop is not.
